cite: DAWIT'S RESTAURANT INC DBA DAVID'S PLACE
summary: The Administrator observes that the Iowa Legislature, through Iowa Code § 123.50(3), has provided mandatory sanctions against a licensee’s license when the licensee or the employee or agent of the licensee is convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).  IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the civil penalty of $500 for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2(h) and the $1,500 civil penalty for the second violation of the section are due and payable to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on or before Thursday, January 22, 2009.  May the licensee avoid the $500 administrative sanction mandated by Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a) by invoking the affirmative defense offered solely through a pilot project of the Alcoholic Beverages Division, when its employee was criminally convicted under Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)?  The Iowa legislature, through Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a), has provided a mandatory $500 civil penalty for a licensee when the licensee or its employee is convicted or found in violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h).  Des Moines, Iowa 50319 Gayle Collins Commissioner Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division 1918 SE Hulsizer Ankeny, Iowa 50021 John Beasley Attorney at Law PO Box 2150 Iowa City, Iowa 52244.

IN RE: : DOCKET NO. D-2008-00034
Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. : DIA NO. 07DOCBL0122
d/b/a David’s Place :
100 S Linn Street : DOCKET NO. D-2007-00140
Iowa City, Iowa 52240 : DIA NO. 08DOCBL014
:
Liquor License No. LC0034106 : ADMINISTRATOR’S FINAL ORDER
______________________________________________________________________________
NOW, on this 17th day of December 2008, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division on the Order to Review the Proposed Decision.
I. STATEMENT OF REVIEW.
The record in this docket discloses that on February 15, 2007, the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages
Division (Division) issued an Order to Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. (Licensee) imposing a $500 civil penalty
for a first conviction of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h), by selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to a
person under the legal age. The violation, which occurred on March 3, 2006, is the Licensee’s first
violation within a two-year period.
The Licensee filed a Notice of Appeal requesting that the Order be reversed and that the civil
penalty be waived. A Notice of Hearing scheduled the matter for a hearing on April 9, 2007. The hearing
was subsequently rescheduled to January 11, 2008.
The record further discloses that on November 8, 2007, the Iowa Department of Public Safety
(DPS) filed an administrative hearing complaint with the Division alleging that on or about February 2,
2007, the Licensee or an employee or agent of the Licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage to an

underage person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The complaint further alleged that the
violation of February 2, 2007, was the second such violation within a period of two years. The matter was
scheduled for a hearing on January 11, 2008, as well.
On January 10, 2008, the matters were consolidated and rescheduled for a hearing on March 7, 2008. On
that date, an administrative hearing was held before an administrative law judge (ALJ) in accordance with
Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123. Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented the Division
on the appeal and the DPS on the hearing complaint. The Licensee was represented by Attorney John
Beasley.
On March 26, 2008, the ALJ issued a Proposed Decision, which imposed a $500 civil penalty
against the Licensee’s license for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) on March 3, 2006, and a
$1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension for the Licensee’s second violation of the section on
February 2, 2007.
On April 25, 2008, the Administrator issued an Order to Review the Proposed Decision on the
Administrator’s own motion to determine if the decision was consistent with agency precedent and
factually supported by the record. The parties were given the opportunity to file exceptions and present
briefs in support of their respective positions. The exceptions and briefs were due no later than the close
of business on May 26, 2008. No exceptions or briefs were filed in the matter.
Upon the motion of a party to the hearing or upon the Administrator’s own motion, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any finding of fact if a preponderance of the evidence will support a
determination to reverse or modify the finding. Iowa Code § 17A.15(3). Moreover, the Administrator
may reverse or modify any conclusion of law that the Administrator finds to be in error. Id.
II. STATEMENT OF LAW.

The alcoholic beverages industry is highly regulated. Iowa Code Chapter 123 was enacted by the
Iowa Legislature “to protect the welfare, health, peace, morals and safety” of Iowans. Iowa Code
§ 123.1. All provisions of Chapter 123 are to be “liberally construed for the accomplishment of that
purpose.” Id. The trafficking of alcoholic beverages affects the public’s interest to the extent that it is
prohibited except as provided in Chapter 123. Id. It is unlawful to manufacture for sale, possess or
transport liquor, wine or beer except under the terms enumerated in Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.2.
“Legal age” is a defined term meaning “twenty-one years of age or more.” Iowa Code
§ 123.3(19). Selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to an underage person, without exercising
“reasonable care to ascertain” whether the person is of the legal drinking age, is a violation of Chapter 123.
Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). A violation of Chapter 123 or the rules of the Division by an employee or
agent of the licensee is deemed an act of the licensee and subjects the licensee’s license to a civil penalty,
suspension or revocation. 185 IAC 4.8.
The administrative penalties for violations of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute. Under
the statute, a first violation of the section “shall” subject a licensee’s license to a civil penalty in the amount
$500.1 Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a). A second violation within two years “shall” subject the license to a
$1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension. Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(b). The penalties become
progressively more severe as the number of sale-to-minor violations increase. A criminal conviction is not
a prerequisite to the imposition of a civil penalty or the suspension or revocation of a license. Iowa Code §
123.39(1)(c).
1 When used in a statute, the word “shall” imposes a duty. Iowa Code § 4.1(30)(a).

When a licensee establishes that a reasonable inquiry was made to determine whether the
purchaser was of legal age, the licensee’s violation of selling the alcoholic beverage to the underage person
is legally excused. Iowa Code § 123.49(3).
III. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES.
A. Did the Licensee satisfy all of the requirements to be eligible for the affirmative defense offered
through the Division sponsored TIPS training program?
B. May the Licensee avoid the $500 civil penalty mandated by Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) by
invoking the affirmative defense offered solely through a pilot project of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages
Division, when the Licensee’s employee was criminally convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h)?
C. Should the Division be precluded or estopped from imposing an administrative sanction for the
Licensee’s first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) because the Licensee relied on the Division’s public
announcement that a one-time affirmative defense would be available through the Division sponsored
TIPS training program if the employee making the sale was TIPS certified?
IV. STATEMENT OF THE FACTS.
On August 4, 2003, the undersigned Administrator issued a press release announcing a server
training program utilizing Training for Interventions Procedures (TIPS) for on-premises licensees located
in Johnson County. The TIPS program is designed to teach servers and sellers of alcoholic beverages how
to prevent underage sales or sales to intoxicated persons. The server training was offered free-of-charge to
licensees through a grant obtained from the Governor’s Traffic Safety Bureau. Proposed Decision, page 3.
The 2003 press release contained the following information about the affirmative defense:
Establishments participating in the TIPS training will be granted a one-time
affirmative defense, valid for a two-year period, whereby a business may avoid civil

prosecution if a sales-to-minor violation occurs in their establishment. In order
for the business to take advantage of the affirmative defense, the employee guilty
of the violation must have been TIPS certified at the time the violation occurred.
Though a business may avoid a civil penalty by asserting the affirmative defense,
the guilty employee will still be subject to a criminal fine.
Licensee’s Exhibit 3. [Emphasis Added].
The Division also circulated brochures promoting the four-hour Johnson County TIPS program.
The brochure stated that the TIPS program could be used by a licensee for a limited period as an
affirmative defense against civil penalties for alcohol sales to minors. The brochure further stated that
licensee or employee cited for selling or providing the alcoholic beverage to the minor could not use the
training as an affirmative defense to avoid the criminal penalties. Proposed Decision, pages 3 and 4.
The training sessions were held in Iowa City during a period commencing on August 4, 2003 and
ending on August 15, 2003. The sessions were taught by certified TIPS trainers from the Division and the
Iowa City Police Department. Certified TIPS trainers from the Sheraton Hotel in Iowa City also
participated in the training. Id.
Dawit Kidane (Kidane) is the manager and 25% shareholder of Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. Kidane
managed Vito’s Bar and Grill in Iowa City for 15 years before opening David’s Place. Christopher
Lindsey (Lindsey) was an employee of Vito’s Bar and Grill during Kidane’s tenure as manager. When
Kidane opened David’s Place, Lindsey left Vito’s to work for Kidane at the new business. Proposed
Decision, page 4. Both Kidane and Lindsey successfully completed the Division sponsored TIPS program
while they were employed at Vito’s Bar and Grill. When Lindsey completed the course on August 8,

2003, a TIPS certification card was issued to him. The card was valid for three years.2 Licensee’s Exhibit
1.
On March 3, 2006, Lindsey was criminally cited for selling an alcoholic beverage to an underage
person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Kidane, who was in the licensed establishment when the
citation was issued, informed the officers that Lindsay was TIPS trained. Kidane believed that by
notifying the officers of the TIPS training, the Licensee would receive the benefit of affirmative defense
offered under the Division’s TIPS training program.
On August 9, 2006, Lindsey voluntarily entered a plea of guilty to the violation without
informing the Licensee of his intention to do so. Lindsey’s guilty plea triggered a $500 civil penalty
against the Licensee’s license for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) within two years. The
penalty was imposed in an Order issued by the Division on February 15, 2007. State’s Exhibit 1.
Kidane was surprised to receive the Order because he had informed officers that Lindsay had been TIPS
trained. Kidane consulted with an attorney, filed an appeal and obtained written confirmation of
Lindsey’s TIPS training. Proposed Decision, page 5.
On February 2, 2007, Iowa City police officers conducted compliance checks to determine whether
establishments would sell or provide an alcoholic beverage to an underage person. Prior to the compliance
checks, the participating informants were required to empty their pockets in the presence of an officer to
ensure that the informants carried only their own valid Iowa driver’s license and the money provided to
them by officers to purchase the alcoholic beverages. Moreover, the informants were instructed to answer
truthfully if asked their age and to provide their own valid Iowa driver’s license if asked for identification.
2 Although the TIPS training certificate was valid for three years, the affirmative defense was available to a licensee for two years
of completing the training program.

Further, each informant was photographed as evidence of their appearance on the night of the compliance
checks. Id.
Shortly after entering the Licensee’s establishment, the officers observed the Licensee’s bartender,
Alisha Hoversten (Hoversten), sell a beer to one of the underage informants without asking for
identification. Hoversten was criminally cited for violating Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Although Kidane
was present in the establishment at the time of the violation, Kidane did not attempt to invoke the
affirmative defense because Hoversten was not TIPS trained. Id.
Hoversten was found not guilty of the charge and the citation against her was dismissed on May
22, 2007. State’s Exhibit 5. The administrative hearing complaint filed by the DPS followed on
November 8, 2007. Proposed Decision, page 6.
The Licensee does not dispute that the Licensee’s employees sold alcoholic beverages to persons
under age 21 during undercover compliance checks on March 3, 2006 and February 2, 2007. Nor does
the Licensee contend that the violation of February 2, 2007, qualifies for the affirmative defense. Rather,
the Licensee asserts that the Licensee is entitled to apply the affirmative defense to the first violation
because the Licensee’s employee had a valid TIPS certification card on March 3, 2006. Proposed
Decision, page 7.
The Licensee further asserts that if the affirmative defense is applied to the first violation, the second
violation would be a first violation making the appropriate administrative sanction a $500 civil
penalty rather than the $1,500 civil penalty and 30-day suspension imposed in the Proposed
Decision. Id.

The State argues that the Licensee is subject to the $500 civil penalty, even though the Licensee’s
employee was TIPS trained, because of the employee’s conviction under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). Moreover, the State asserts that because Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) provides a mandatory
penalty, the Division has no authority to allow the affirmative defense provided under the pilot project.
The affirmative defense is available only when a licensee or employee is acquitted or found guilty under an
alternate code section. Thus, the sale-to-minor violation of February 2, 2007, is a second violation and the
administrative sanction of a $1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension is mandated by Iowa
Code § 123.50(3)(b). Proposed Decision, page 8.
The Licensee counters that the Division should be precluded from imposing an administrative
sanction for the violation of March 3, 2006, because the Division failed to inform licensees that in order to
claim the affirmative defense, the licensee had to ensure that the person who committed the violation was
not convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Kidane contends that if the information had been
provided to him, he would have hired an attorney to represent Lindsey in the criminal case. Id.
V. ANALYSIS.
A. Program Eligibility
An issue indirectly raised is whether the Licensee satisfied all of the requirements to be eligible for
the affirmative defense offered through the Division sponsored TIPS training program. The record
reflects that Lindsey successfully completed the Division sponsored TIPS training on August 8, 2003, and
received a TIPS certificate valid for a three-year period.
The affirmative defense offered under the Division sponsored program was valid for two years from
completion of the program. Proposed Decision, page 4; Licensee Exhibit 1. The information distributed
by the Division to promote the program stated that licensed establishments participating in

the Division sponsored TIPS training program would be granted a one-time affirmative defense
valid for a “two-year period.”
The Administrator observes that the affirmative defense available to the Licensee for any underage
violations committed by Lindsey would have expired on August 7, 2005.3 The date of the underage
violation committed by Lindsey was March 2, 2006 – nearly 7 months beyond the last day the affirmative
defense was valid. The Administrator notes that, even if Lindsey had not been convicted under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h), the affirmative defense was no longer valid and would not have applied in the case.
While the answer to the first issue effectively resolves this appeal, the remaining issues will be
addressed to clarify the affirmative defense in future cases.
B. Effect of a Criminal Conviction.
The ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence established that the Licensee violated Iowa
Code § 123.49(2)(h) a second time when Hoversten sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage informant
on February 2, 2007. The sale occurred under controlled circumstances with officers present. The
Licensee does not dispute that Hoversten made the prohibited sale on that date and offered no defense to
the violation.
At the hearing, the focus of the issue between the parties was whether the Licensee may successfully assert
the affirmative defense for the violation of March 3, 2006, when Lindsey was convicted under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). The Administrator observes that the Iowa Legislature, through Iowa Code § 123.50(3),
has provided mandatory sanctions against a licensee’s license when the licensee or the employee or agent of
the licensee is convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The Legislature has not provided any
3 The Division offered a second round to TIPS training, with the renewed affirmative defense commencing, on August 4, 2003,
and ending on August 15, 2003.

exceptions to the statute and the Division has not promulgated any rules providing an exception or an
affirmative defense to the statutory sanction. As such, the affirmative
defense is only an option when a licensee or a licensee’s employees or agents have not been
convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
C. Doctrine of Estoppel.
The Licensee also rgues that the Division should be estopped from imposing a sanction for the
violation because the Division’s public announcements failed to inform licensees that the affirmative
defense could not be applied when there was a conviction under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Id.
Essentially, Kidane argues that the Division should be estopped from imposing a $500 civil
penalty for the violation of March 3, 2006, because the press release and brochure announcing the
affirmative defense misled the Licensee. The doctrine of equitable estoppel is a common law doctrine
preventing one party who has made certain representations from taking unfair advantage of another when
the party making the representations changes its position to the prejudice of the party who relied upon the
representations. Ahrendsen v. Iowa Dep’t of Human Servs., 613 N.W.2d 674, 678 (Iowa 2000). The
elements of equitable estoppel are: (1) a false representation or concealment of material facts; (2) a lack of
knowledge of the true facts on the part of the actor; (3) the intention that it be acted upon; and (4)
reliance thereon by the party to whom made, to his prejudice and injury. ABD Disposal Systems, Inc. v.
Department of Natural Resources, 681 N.W.2d 596, 606 (Iowa 2004).
The general rule is that estoppel does not lie against a government agency absent extraordinary
circumstances. Bailiff v. Adams County Conference Bd., 650 N.W.2d 621, 627 (Iowa 2002). A person
seeking to invoke the doctrine of equitable estoppel against a government body “bears a heavy burden,

particularly when the government acts in a sovereign or governmental role rather than a proprietary role.”
Id. In addressing the application of the doctrine of equitable estoppel to government action, the Iowa
Supreme Court found that parties are charged with knowledge of the law and cannot ignore the plain
meaning of the law. Iowa Department of Transportation v. Nebraska-Iowa Supply Co., 272 N.W.2d 6, 14
(Iowa 1978).
The ALJ found that the Licensee did not carry the heavy burden of establishing that the Division
should be equitably estopped from imposing a $500 civil penalty for Lindsey’s sale-to-minor violation on
March 3, 2006. Moreover, the ALJ found, “While the Division’s written announcements of the pilot
project should have explained that the affirmative defense could not be asserted if the employee was
convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h), there was no showing that the omission of this information
from the press release or brochure was intentional and not just a mistake or an oversight. Iowa Code §
123.50(3)(a) is controlling and requires the imposition of the $500 civil penalty in this case.” Proposed
Decision, page 10.
Further, the ALJ found that by imposing the $500 civil penalty, “the Division Administrator is
clearly acting in his governmental role, in compliance with the statutory duties and obligations assigned to
him. The Division Administrator does not have the authority to waive or disregard the statute when
implementing the pilot project.” The $500 civil penalty imposed for the first violation of Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h) is mandated by statute and must be imposed for the violation of March 3, 2006.
The ALJ further found that the Licensee violated Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) a second time on
February 2, 2007, when the Licensee’s employee sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage person. The

Licensee neither disputed the violation, nor offered a defense to the violation. The violation of February
2, 2007, triggers the mandatory sanctions provided under Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(b).
VI. ORDER.
For the above-stated reasons, the Administrator of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division FINDS
that the administrative sanctions imposed in the Proposed Decision of March 26, 2008, should be
AFFIRMED.
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and the Decision
and Order proposed by the administrative law judge are AFFIRMED and incorporated herein in their
entirety.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the civil penalty of $500 for the first violation of Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2(h) and the $1,500 civil penalty for the second violation of the section are due and payable to
the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on or before
Thursday, January 22, 2009. Failure to pay the civil penalties by that date shall result in further
administrative proceedings against liquor license number LC0034106.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that liquor license number LC0034106, issue to Dawit’s
Restaurant, Inc., located at 100 S. Linn Street in Iowa City, Iowa is suspended for a period of 30 days
commencing at 6 AM on Thursday, January 22, 2009, and ending at 6 AM on Saturday, February 21,
2009. The Licensee is hereby notified that liquor, wine and beer shall not be consumed in or on the
licensed premises located at 100 S. Linn Street in Iowa City, Iowa during the period of the suspension.
The premises may be used for other lawful purposes during the suspension.

The parties are hereby notified that this Order constitutes final agency action for the purpose of
Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final, unless a party to the hearing files a Petition
for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court within 30 days from the date of this Order. Iowa Code §
17A.19.
DATED this 17th of December 2008, Ankeny, Iowa.

On February 15, 2007, the Iowa Department of
Commerce-Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) issued an
Order to Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. d/b/a David’s Place
(licensee), which required the licensee to pay a civil
penalty of $500 for a first conviction of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h) [sale to underage person] within a period of
two years. The licensee appealed from the assessment of
the civil penalty, and a hearing was scheduled for April 9,
2007. The hearing was continued twice at the licensee's
request and was eventually rescheduled for January 11,
2008.
On November 8, 2007, the Iowa Department of Public Safety
(DPS) filed an administrative hearing complaint with the
Iowa Department of Commerce-Alcoholic Beverages Division
(Division). The hearing complaint alleged that on or about
February 2, 2007, the licensee or an employee or agent of
the licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to an underage person, in violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). The hearing complaint further alleged
that this was the licensee’s second violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h) within a period of two years. A
hearing was scheduled for January 11, 2008.
On January 10, 2008, the two hearings were consolidated and
continued to March 7, 2008. On January 11, 2008, the
undersigned received a letter from Christopher Lindsey, a
former employee of the licensee. Copies of the letter had
also been sent to both parties.

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 2
The hearing was held before the undersigned administrative
law judge on March 7, 2008 at 10:00 a.m. at the office of
the Iowa Department of Commerce, Alcoholic Beverages
Division, 1918 S.E. Hulsizer, Ankeny, Iowa. Assistant
Attorney General John Lundquist represented both the
Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) on the appeal and
the Department of Public Safety (DPS) on the hearing
complaint. Attorney John Beasley represented the licensee.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Notice of Hearing Before
Administrator’s Designee; Motions for Continuance; Hearing
Complaint, Notice of Hearing, Continuance
Order/Consolidation Order; Christopher Lindsey letter dated
1/8/08; the testimony of the witnesses, and the following
exhibits:
State Exhibit 1: Order Imposing $500 Civil Penalty,
2/15/07 and attachments
State Exhibit 2: Citation and Disposition, State v.
Christopher Lindsey
State Exhibit 3: Iowa City Police Incident Report,
2/2/07
State Exhibit 4: Voluntary Statement, 2/2/07
State Exhibit 5: Citation and Disposition, State v.
Alisha Hoversten
State Exhibit 6: Liquor License Information
Licensee Exhibit 1: Letter Confirming TIPS training
for Christopher Lindsey, 5/31/2007
Licensee Exhibit 2: Division Information/Brochures re:
TIPS training
Licensee Exhibit 3: Information on Division Website
re: TIPS Pilot Project
ISSUES
May the licensee avoid the $500 administrative sanction
mandated by Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a) by invoking the
affirmative defense offered solely through a pilot project
of the Alcoholic Beverages Division, when its employee was
criminally convicted under Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)?
Should the Division be precluded or estopped from imposing
an administrative sanction for the licensee’s first
violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) because the

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 3
licensee relied on the Division’s public announcement that
a one-time affirmative defense would be available if the
employee making the sale was TIPS certified?
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Dawit’s Restaurant Inc. d/b/a David’s Place
(licensee), holds Liquor License No. LC-34106 for the
premises located at 100 S. Linn Street in Iowa City, Iowa.
Dawit Kidane is a 25% owner of Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. and
is the manager of David’s Place. Prior to opening David’s
Place in 2006, Mr. Kidane managed Vito’s in Iowa City for
15 years. (Testimony of Dawit Kidane; State Exhibit 6)
2. On August 4, 2003, the Division Administrator issued a
press release announcing a new alcoholic beverages server
training pilot project utilizing Training for Intervention
Procedures (TIPS). TIPS is a training program designed to
assist employees of bars and restaurants to avoid or
prevent alcohol sales to minors or intoxicated patrons.
The pilot project was funded by the Iowa Governor’s Traffic
Safety Bureau, and the Division offered the TIPS training
free of charge to all on-premises liquor licensees in
Johnson County.
The Division’s press release further stated:
Establishments participating in the TIPS training
will be granted a one-time affirmative defense,
valid for a two-year period, whereby a business
may avoid civil prosecution if a sales-to-minors
violation occurs in their establishment. In
order for the business to take advantage of the
affirmative defense, the employee guilty of the
violation must have been TIPS certified at the
time the violation occurred. Though a business
may avoid a civil penalty by asserting the
affirmative defense, the guilty employee would
still be subject to a criminal fine.
(Licensee Exhibit 3)
The Division also provided registration forms and brochures
for the four-hour TIPS training sessions in Iowa City. The
brochure also stated that TIPS training may be used by a
licensee for a limited period as an affirmative defense
against civil penalties for alcohol sales to minors and

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 4
that the employee cited for alcohol sales to minors may not
use training as an affirmative defense and will be subject
to the same criminal penalties as those not TIPS certified.
(Licensee Exhibit 2)
639 employees of 53 Johnson County establishments attended
the TIPS training sessions that were held in Iowa City from
August 4-15, 2003. The training sessions were taught by
TIPS certified trainers from the Division, from the Iowa
City Police Department, and from the Iowa City Sheraton
Hotel. (Licensee Exhibit 3)
3. Christopher Lindsey, an employee of Vito’s Bar and
Grill in Iowa City, successfully completed the TIPS
Training Course on August 8, 2003. According to the Iowa
City Police Department, Mr. Lindsey was issued a training
certificate valid for a period of three years.1 (Licensee
Exhibit 1) Dawit Kidane also received TIPS training while
employed at Vito’s. David’s Place, which is an Ethiopian
restaurant, opened for business on or about March 2, 2006.
Christopher Lindsey left Vito’s to work for Dawit Kidane at
David’s Place. (Testimony of Dawit Kidane; Licensee
Exhibits 2, 3)
4. The licensee does not dispute that employee
Christopher Lindsey was issued a criminal citation for
selling an alcoholic beverage to an underage person on
March 3, 2006, in violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h). Dawit Kidane was present in the restaurant
at the time of the sale and told the officers issuing the
citation that Christopher Lindsey was TIPS trained. Mr.
Kidane was under the impression that this was all that he
needed to do in order for the licensee to receive the
benefit of the affirmative defense to a civil penalty for
the prohibited sale.
In May or June 2006, Christopher Lindsey moved to Chicago
and resigned from his employment at David’s Place. On
August 9, 2006, Mr. Lindsey entered a guilty plea in
1 A three-year certificate appears inconsistent with the two-year period
for asserting the affirmative defense that is cited in the Division’s
press release and brochure. The Division’s attorney stated that while
the training certificates were issued for three years, the affirmative

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
I. Applicable Statutes and Rules
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2005, 2007) provides:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control
license or retail wine or beer permit under this
chapter, and the person's or club's agents or
employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any
alcoholic beverage, wine or beer to any person,
knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under legal age,
or permit any person, knowing or failing to
exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the
person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of
age or more. Iowa Code section 123.3(19)(2005, 2007).
A violation of the Act or the rules of the division by any
employee, agent or servant of a licensee or permittee shall
be deemed to be the act of the licensee or permittee and
shall subject the license or permit of said licensee or
permittee to suspension or revocation. 185 IAC 4.8. A
criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension,
revocation, or imposition of a civil penalty. Iowa Code
section 123.39(1)(c).
Iowa Code section 123.50 (2005, 2007) provides, in relevant
part:
123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.

is not a prerequisite to the imposition of a civil penalty)

II. Summary of the Parties’ Positions
The licensee did not dispute that its employees sold
alcohol to underage persons during undercover compliance
operations on March 3, 2006 and again on February 2, 2007.
Nor does the licensee contend that the second sale
qualified for the affirmative defense. Rather, the
licensee asserts that it is entitled to the affirmative
defense on the first sale because that employee had a valid
certificate of TIPS training at the time of the sale. The
licensee further asserts that if the affirmative defense is
applied to the first sale, then the second sale should only
trigger the $500 civil penalty sanction applicable to a
first violation, not the 30-day license suspension and
$1500 civil penalty applicable to a second violation.
The state maintains that the licensee is subject to the
mandatory $500 civil penalty for the first sale, even

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 8
though the employee had TIPS training, because the employee
was convicted under Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h). The
state asserts that because Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a)
provides a mandatory penalty, the Division lacks discretion
to allow the pilot project’s affirmative defense. The
state further contends that the affirmative defense is only
available if the employee is acquitted or pled guilty under
a different code section, such as Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(j) or a municipal ordinance, thereby avoiding the
application of Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a).3 Finally,
the state asserts that the subsequent violation on February
7, 2007 is therefore a second violation, which triggers the
mandatory administrative sanction of a $1500 civil penalty
and a 30-day license suspension. See Iowa Code section
123.50(3)(a) and (b).
The licensee responds that the Division should be precluded
from imposing an administrative sanction for the March 3,
2006 violation because its public announcement of the
affirmative defense failed to inform liquor licensees that
in order to claim it, they had to ensure that their
employee was not convicted under Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h). Dawit Kidane contends that if this
information had been provided to him, he would have hired a
lawyer to represent his employee on the citation.
III. Analysis
The licensee’s employee, Christopher Lindsey, pled guilty
to a violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) based on
his sale of an alcoholic beverage to a nineteen-year-old
female on March 3, 2006. The Iowa legislature, through
Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a), has provided a mandatory
$500 civil penalty for a licensee when the licensee or its
employee is convicted or found in violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). The legislature has not provided any
exceptions to this statute nor has the Division promulgated
any rules providing for an exception or an affirmative
defense to the statutory sanction.
3 According to statements made by the attorneys in support of their
continuance requests and at hearing, Iowa City and at least some
licensees were aware of this roadblock to claiming the affirmative
defense, and some licensees have avoided this problem because their
employee was not prosecuted, received a deferred judgment, or negotiated
a plea under a different code provision. (See Continuance
Order/Consolidation Order issued 1/10/08; Lindsey Letter dated 1/8/08)

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 9
In August 2003, the Division announced its Johnson County
pilot project to offer the affirmative defense in
conjunction with TIPS training. Apparently the only
written documentation of the affirmative defense was
through the press release posted on the Division’s website
and through the TIPS training program brochures and/or
training materials. This written documentation states that
establishments will be granted a “one-time affirmative
defense, valid for a two-year period.” In order for the
business to take advantage of the affirmative defense, the
employee guilty of the violation must have been TIPS
certified at the time the violation occurred. When
Christopher Lindsey made the prohibited sale on March 3,
2006, his three-year training certificate was still valid,
but it had been more than two years since he completed his
TIPS training. A literal reading of the press release and
brochure suggests that Mr. Lindsey’s training, more than
two years prior to the sale, does not permit assertion of
the affirmative defense. However, since the state conceded
that Mr. Lindsey fell within the affirmative defense
two-year window, this proposed decision will presume that
Mr. Lindsey’s training was timely.4
The fighting issue between the parties is whether the
licensee may successfully assert the affirmative defense
for the first violation when Christopher Lindsey was
convicted under Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h). Neither
the press release nor the brochures speak to the mandatory
administrative sanctions triggered under Iowa Code section
123.50(3) when the employee is convicted under Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). It is unclear whether the TIPS
training materials or lectures addressed the problem that
123.50(3) poses to the assertion of the affirmative
defense. Dawit Kidane could not recall that he was ever
advised that the affirmative defense was not available if
the employee was convicted under Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h).
Essentially, the licensee argues that it was misled by the
Division’s public announcements of the affirmative defense
and that the Division should now be estopped from assessing
the $500 civil penalty for the March 3, 2006 violation.
The doctrine of equitable estoppel is a common law doctrine
preventing one party who has made certain representations
4 However, the licensee’s suggestion that the affirmative defense is
available once every two years is rejected as clearly contrary to the
language used in the press release and the brochure.

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 10
from taking unfair advantage of another when the party
making the representations changes its position to the
prejudice of the party who relied upon the representations.
Ahrendsen v. Iowa Dep’t of Human Servs., 613 N.W.2d 674,
678 (Iowa 2000). The elements of equitable estoppel are:
(1) a false representation or concealment of material
facts; (2) lack of knowledge of the true facts on the part
of the actor; (3) the intention that it be acted upon; and
(4) reliance thereon by the party to whom made, to his
prejudice and injury. ABC Disposal Systems, Inc. v.
Department of Natural Resources, 681 N.W.2d 596, 606 (Iowa
2004).
The general rule is that estoppel does not lie against a
government agency absent extraordinary circumstances.
Bailiff v. Adams County Conference Bd., 650 N.W.2d 621,627
(Iowa 2002). A person seeking to invoke the doctrine of
equitable estoppel against a government body “bears a heavy
burden, particularly when the government acts in a
sovereign or governmental role rather than a proprietary
role.” Id. Moreover, in addressing the application of
the doctrine of equitable estoppel to government action,
the Supreme Court has found that parties are charged with
knowledge of the law and cannot ignore the plain meaning of
the law. See Iowa Department of Transportation v.
Nebraska-Iowa Supply Co., 272 N.W.2d 6, 14 (Iowa 1978)
(holding that despite representations by the Department of
Transportation’s engineer that the Department would share
the costs of installing a culvert, plaintiff could not rely
representations made by the engineer when there was no
statutory basis for liability.)
The licensee has not carried its heavy burden to establish
that the Division should be equitably estopped from
assessing the $500 civil penalty for the violation on March
3, 2006. While the Division’s written announcements of the
pilot project should have explained that the affirmative
defense could not be asserted if the employee was convicted
under Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h), there was no showing
that the omission of this information from the press
release or brochure was intentional and not just a mistake
or an oversight. Moreover, Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a)
is controlling and requires the imposition of the $500
civil penalty in this case. The licensee is charged with
knowledge of the statute. By imposing the $500 civil
penalty, the Division Administrator is clearly acting in
his governmental role, in compliance with the statutory

DIA No. 07DOCBL014,086
Page 11
duties and obligations assigned to him. The Division
Administrator does not have the authority to waive or
disregard the statute when implementing the pilot project.
The $500 civil penalty mandated by Iowa Code section
123.50(30(a) must be applied to the first violation on
March 3, 2006.
The preponderance of the evidence established that the
licensee violated Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) a second
time when its employee sold an alcoholic beverage to an
underage person on February 2, 2007. Undercover officers
witnessed the sale to an underage female during a
controlled alcohol compliance check. The licensee did not
dispute that its employee made a prohibited sale on this
date and offered no defenses to this violation. Since this
was a second violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)
within a period of two years, the mandatory sanctions under
Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(b) must be assessed.
